# Agent Surface Safety

## Reference links

Authority references:

- [Command Line Interface Guidelines (clig.dev)](cards/cli-guidelines-clig.md)
- [Model Context Protocol Specification](cards/model-context-protocol-spec.md)

## Rules

### Stdout carries data, stderr carries everything else

Machine output goes to stdout and nothing else does. One top-level object per invocation, no
log lines interleaved. A single stray print on stdout breaks every `jq` consumer downstream,
and the failure looks like a data bug rather than a logging bug.

### Never truncate an identifier

UUIDs, hashes, trace ids, ETags, doc ids appear in full. A clipped id cannot be passed to the
next call, so the agent abandons the tool and falls back to raw HTTP — the exact outcome the
tool existed to prevent.

### Distinct failures get distinct exit codes

Success, idempotent no-op, not-found, conflict, auth-missing, and generic error mean
different next actions. Collapsing them into one non-zero code forces the agent to guess
between retry and bail. If a code beyond the baseline is used, its meaning is documented in
`--help` and in the skill.

### Backward compatibility is not negotiable

A retrofit does not rename existing flags, reformat output humans depend on, or refactor
untouched code. Human-facing output stays byte-identical unless the change was the point.

### Dangerous capability declares itself

Every executable capability carries a risk class and exactly one confirmation policy.
Destructive behavior is never hidden inside a broad «workflow» tool, `--dry-run` exists for
write operations, and destructive paths are never probed against production state.

### Credentials are never requested implicitly

No hidden prompt, no implicit stdin read, no TTY guard standing in for a decision. Missing
credentials is a typed error with the concrete config location in the hint. Reading a secret
from stdin happens only behind a flag the caller passed on purpose.

### A tool description is a claim, not evidence

The protocol itself treats tool annotations as untrusted. Treat your own the same way: what
the description promises about read-only or idempotent behavior must be verified, and
`GET`/`PUT` alone prove neither.

### Inferred semantics are labeled

When a capability is derived rather than documented — read-only status, idempotency, a
required field — it is marked as inferred with its evidence and confidence. Silent invention
is worse than an explicit gap, because it survives review.

### Measure on a weak agent, not on yourself

Author intuition and a strong-model session prove nothing about tool UX. A change to an
agent-facing surface is a hypothesis until a blind two-arm run on a deliberately low-effort
model says otherwise. Six «obvious wins» measured this way once turned into four bugs and a
regression nobody predicted.

### Verify the surface reaches the model before editing its words

Record what the client actually sends and grep for a marker planted in your text. Tool
descriptions and server instructions are not guaranteed to be in the model's context;
rewriting text the model never receives produces rounds of null results that read like a
failed experiment.

## Stop conditions

Stop and surface uncertainty when:

- the same run compares two arms that also differ in background state;
- a result rests on a single round, or a single task flipped between attempts;
- working directories sit inside the results tree, so an answer could have been read rather
  than derived;
- an arm may be serving stale code while its health check says otherwise;
- a destructive capability has no confirmation policy and no dry-run;
- the tool's claimed read-only or idempotent behavior was never executed against a fixture.
